Tolkien and the rewrite of the Ring Cycle

I'm sorry to say it, but that review is so full of wrong assumptions and failures it's painful. It was clearly written by someone unfamiliar with the Northern European mythologies.

Tolkien was very interested in Norse mythology and the Icelandic Sagas, as well as many other branches of old Nordic and Germanic, Anglo-Saxon mythology. Wagner of course was the same, and this leads to similarities in their works, similarities that have nothing to do with Tolkien.

But the parallels between the two works are so extensive as to raise the question as to Tolkien’s intent.

Nope, nope they aren't.

The inspiration for the ring of power comes in large part from the Völsunga Saga both for Wagner and Tolkien, no cross-over between the two, just the same sources.

Wotan uses the Ring to pay the giants. Sauron betrays the Elves. // Wotan needs the giants to build Valhalla. The Elves need Sauron to forge their Rings of Power

These aren't similarities, but differences!

Siegfried inherits the shards of his father’s sword. Aragorn inherits the shards of his fathers’ sword

Again, this is from Norse mythology where Odin gives Gramr to Sigismund, Odin later breaks Gramr, Sigurd inherits the shards of Gramr, and the sword is later reforged. It is then used to kill a mighty dragon who guards a mighty hoard, in which there is a ring of power. All that is from Norse Mythology, not "The Ring Cycle"

We can also look at these "similarities" ||The immortals burn in Valhalla. The immortals leave Middle-earth|| ||A new era emerges in the world. A new era emerges in the world|| ||Men are left to their own devices. Men are left to their own devices||

But oh wait! In Norse mythology the Gods all die in the big battle of Ragnarok, with only two humans surviving, who then go on to live in a "reborn" world, left to their own devices. Sort of a garden of Eden, Adam and Eve type of situation.

The ideas underlying the two works are radically different, drawing from the radically different thoughts and morals of the two authors. And whatever similarities there are, all reach back to Anglo-Saxon, Norse, and German mythology. It has nothing to do with Tolkien trying to imitate Wagner, or improve upon his work, that Tolkien disliked Wagner can be taken at face value, and that he should somehow be trying to repair or otherwise "rework" Wagners work is silly.
